overview.intro: Two accountants can be given identical transactions and produce different profits unless they share a set of rules about when to recognise revenue, what to treat as an asset and how to disclose. Those rules are the accounting concepts and conventions, and together they form the generally accepted accounting principles known as GAAP. This unit sets out the major concepts, contrasts the cash basis with the accrual basis on which financial statements are actually built, explains the role of accounting standards in removing differences between firms, and introduces international financial reporting standards as the global convergence point. The examinable skill is applying the right concept to a given treatment and justifying it.

learningOutcomes: Explain the meaning and need for generally accepted accounting principles.
Apply the principal accounting concepts to given transactions.
Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis of accounting.
State the purpose of accounting standards and give examples.
Describe IFRS, its need and its basic assumptions.

learn.title: GAAP and the principal accounting concepts

blocks.text: Generally accepted accounting principles are the body of rules, concepts and conventions that determine how financial statements are prepared and reported. They exist so that a reader can compare one firm with another and one year with the next without relearning the basis each time. The business entity concept keeps the owner’s private affairs out of the firm. The going concern concept assumes the business will continue indefinitely, which is what justifies carrying assets at cost rather than at scrap value. Money measurement admits only events that can be expressed in money. The accounting period concept fixes a year as the interval for reporting results.

blocks.caption: Principal accounting concepts and the treatment each requires
rows: The firm is separate from its owner
Drawings are not treated as an expense
Assets are not valued at forced-sale prices
Staff morale is never quantified in the ledger
Results are reported for a fixed period
Depreciation and accruals are made yearly
Assets are recorded at purchase cost
Anticipate no profit, provide for all losses
Closing stock at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower
Ignore items too small to influence decisions
Stamp paper expensed instead of capitalised
Depreciation method does not change arbitrarily

items.text: The proprietor pays for a family holiday from the business bank account.
items.note: The entity concept requires the amount to be recorded as drawings, not as a business expense.

items.text: A patent bought for ₹2,00,000 is now worth ₹5,00,000 in the market.
items.note: The cost concept keeps it at ₹2,00,000 in the books; the gain is not recognised until the asset is sold.

learn.title: Cash basis and accrual basis of accounting

blocks.text: The cash basis records a transaction only when money actually changes hands. Rent is an expense in the month it is paid, and a sale is income in the month the customer pays. It is simple and it cannot be manipulated easily, but it produces a misleading profit: a firm that buys stock in December and collects in January shows a wonderful December simply because it paid nothing. The accrual basis, which is what GAAP requires, records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, irrespective of when cash moves. Under accrual, goods sold in March are March revenue even if the money arrives in June, and the electricity used in March is a March expense even if the bill is settled in April.

blocks.caption: Cash basis against accrual basis
rows: Record only when cash is paid or received
Distorts profit between periods; not allowed under GAAP
Matches revenue to the period; comparable
Requires adjustments such as accruals and prepayments

blocks.text: The adjustments needed to move from cash records to accrual statements are the practical heart of this concept: outstanding expenses are added, prepaid expenses are deducted, income received in advance is deducted, income accrued but not received is added, and depreciation is charged as a non-cash allocation. Each of these exists because the cash has not moved on the date the economic event occurred.

items.text: Salary of ₹30,000 is paid in April covering March and April at ₹15,000 each.
items.note: Under accrual, ₹15,000 belongs to March as an outstanding liability and ₹15,000 to April as the expense of that month.

items.text: Commission of ₹12,000 is received in March for a service completed in April.
items.note: Under accrual this is income received in advance and is shown as a liability until April, not as March income.

blocks.text: Accounting standards are the specific rules issued by a recognised body to standardise treatment, disclosure and presentation. In India the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India issues them as AS, and companies listed on stock exchanges follow the Indian Accounting Standards Ind AS which converge with international practice. Standards exist because concepts alone leave discretion: two firms may both follow conservatism yet disclose differently. A standard fixes the treatment and the note that must accompany it, so that a reader comparing two balance sheets is comparing like with like.

items: AS 1 requires a disclosure of accounting policies followed consistently.
AS 6 deals with depreciation and makes the method and rate explicit.
AS 10 requires fixed assets to be stated at cost less accumulated depreciation.
AS 2 governs the valuation of inventory, including the lower of cost and net realisable value rule.
AS 9 governs revenue recognition, tying revenue to the transfer of significant risks and rewards.
AS 22 deals with taxes on income, matching deferred tax with the timing difference that caused it.

blocks.text: A firm must disclose any departure from a standard and give both the reason for the departure and its financial effect, which is why the notes to the accounts form part of the statements rather than being decoration. Where two standards appear to conflict, the more specific requirement prevails, and the policies adopted must be applied consistently to similar items in every period unless a change is required by a newer standard and is disclosed with its effect.

learn.title: International Financial Reporting Standards: meaning, need and assumptions

blocks.text: IFRS is a set of standards issued by the International Accounting Standards Board that aims to make financial statements comparable across countries. Its need arises from global capital: an investor in Mumbai reading a German company’s report needs the same rules of recognition and measurement that apply at home, or the comparison is meaningless. Convergence also reduces the cost of preparing two sets of statements for a firm listed in more than one market. IFRS is principles based rather than rule based, which gives professional judgement a larger role and therefore puts more weight on disclosure.

blocks.caption: Foundational assumptions of IFRS
rows: Revenue and expenses are recognised when earned or incurred, not when cash moves
The entity is expected to continue operating for the foreseeable future
The reporting currency is assumed stable enough for statement presentation
The same format and classification are used across periods
Financial statements give a true and fair view of the entity’s position and performance

items: IFRS allows fewer exceptions and more uniform disclosure than national standards.
Recognition of assets and liabilities focuses on control and future economic benefit.
Measurement often uses fair value where national standards would use historic cost.
A single set of statements lowers reporting cost for multinational businesses.
India’s Ind AS standards are converged with IFRS with only narrow, notified differences.

figures.caption: Figure: The hierarchy from concepts to financial statements
figures.description: A four-tier pyramid: at the base the accounting concepts and conventions, above them GAAP, then the accounting standards issued by the national body, and at the apex the published financial statements.
labels: Concepts: entity, going concern, accrual, conservatism
GAAP: the generally accepted body of principle
Accounting standards: AS or Ind AS fixing specific treatments
Financial statements: prepared under the framework above them

keyPoints: GAAP is the body of accepted principles that makes statements comparable across firms and years.
The business entity concept separates the owner’s drawings from business expenses.
Going concern justifies carrying assets at cost rather than at liquidation value.
The cost concept prevents market price rises from being recorded as profit before a sale.
Conservatism requires no anticipated profit but full provision for known losses.
Consistency requires the same method year after year so that trends mean something.
The cash basis records only on movement of cash and is not permitted for financial statements.
The accrual basis records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred.
Accounting standards issued by the ICAI standardise recognition, measurement and disclosure.
IFRS aims at global comparability and is principles based with fair presentation at its centre.
examFocus: Concept questions are answered by naming the concept, defining it in one line and applying it to the item in the question; definition alone earns only part marks.
Cash versus accrual questions usually give a paid-in-advance or paid-in-arrears item, so show the split across the two periods.
Justify an accounting treatment by quoting the concept that requires it, not merely by stating what is done.

vocabulary.meaning: Generally accepted accounting principles, the shared rules for preparing financial statements.
Recording revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, independent of cash movement.
Recording transactions only when cash is actually received or paid.
Assumption that the business will continue operating for the foreseeable future.
Judgement that an item is significant enough to influence a reader’s decision.
Applying the same accounting treatment from one period to the next.
International Financial Reporting Standards issued by the IASB for global comparability.

questions.prompt: Under the accrual basis, revenue is recorded:
options: When it is earned, whatever the cash position
At the end of the financial year only
questions.answer: When it is earned, whatever the cash position
questions.explanation: Accrual recognition follows the earning of the revenue and the incurring of the expense, not the movement of cash.

questions.prompt: A business values its closing stock at cost even though the market price has risen sharply. This follows the:
questions.explanation: The cost concept requires assets to be carried at purchase cost, and an unrealised market rise is not recognised as profit.

questions.prompt: The proprietor withdrew ₹50,000 for personal use. Which concept requires this to be recorded as drawings?
questions.explanation: The entity concept treats the owner and the business as separate persons, so personal spending is a reduction of capital and never an expense.

questions.prompt: Which pair of concepts most directly justifies writing an obsolete machine down to its realisable value?
questions.explanation: A departure from going concern combined with conservatism requires a loss to be provided for as soon as it is known, rather than carrying the asset at cost.

questions.prompt: The body of accepted principles that allows one firm’s statements to be compared with another’s is known by the initials __________ .
questions.explanation: Generally accepted accounting principles give a common basis, so differences between statements reflect real differences and not different rules.

questions.prompt: Expenses incurred during a period but not yet paid at the end of it are called __________ expenses.
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting adds outstanding expenses in the profit and loss account and shows them as a liability in the balance sheet.

questions.prompt: State four generally accepted accounting concepts and give one line of explanation for each.
questions.answer: Business entity: the firm is separate from its owner. Going concern: the business is assumed to continue indefinitely. Money measurement: only transactions measurable in money are recorded. Accounting period: results are reported for a fixed interval of a year. Consistency: the same method is used from year to year.
questions.explanation: Four concepts with a correct one-line explanation each earn full marks; naming concepts without explanation earns half.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the cash basis from the accrual basis of accounting.
questions.answer: The cash basis records revenue and expenses only when cash is actually received or paid, so it reports the cash movement of the period. The accrual basis records revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred irrespective of cash movement, which matches costs to the revenue they helped generate. The accrual basis is required for financial statements because it gives a comparable profit figure.
questions.explanation: The distinction must be drawn on the timing of recognition, and the answer should state which basis GAAP requires.

questions.prompt: Explain the meaning and need for accounting standards and give any three examples.
questions.answer: Accounting standards are specific authoritative rules issued by a recognised body, in India the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, that prescribe the recognition, measurement, presentation and disclosure of transactions. Their need arises because broad concepts still leave room for discretion: without them two firms with identical transactions could report different profits and assets. Standards remove that discretion and make statements comparable, comparable across firms and across years, and they reduce reporting cost for companies operating in more than one market. Examples are AS 1 on disclosure of accounting policies, AS 6 on depreciation, AS 2 on the valuation of inventory, AS 9 on revenue recognition and AS 22 on taxes on income.
questions.explanation: Full marks need both the definition and the need, supported by correctly named standards; examples alone do not answer the why.

questions.prompt: Goods worth ₹80,000 are sold in March, invoiced on 30 March and the customer pays on 15 April. Rent of ₹24,000 for January to March is paid on 10 April. State how each is treated under the cash basis and under the accrual basis for the year ending 31 March.
questions.answer: Under the accrual basis, the sale of ₹80,000 is revenue of the year ending 31 March because the risks and rewards passed at invoicing, and it appears as a debtor of ₹80,000 in the balance sheet; the rent of ₹24,000 is an expense of that year as an outstanding liability of ₹24,000, since ₹8,000 belongs to January, February and March at ₹8,000 a month. Under the cash basis, neither affects the year: the sale falls into April when the money arrives, and the rent falls into April when it is paid, so the profit of the year to 31 March excludes both entirely.
questions.explanation: The answer must handle four items across two bases: sale and rent under accrual, then both deferred into April under cash, showing why the cash basis misstates performance.
